title: Agentic AI for Business
tagline: Understand, plan, govern and deploy AI agents that do real work safely, from the first pilot to a scaled fleet.
description:
AI has moved beyond chatbots that answer questions. **AI agents** can now plan steps, call business systems, look up documents and take actions towards a goal. Used well, they shorten turnaround times and free skilled people for judgement work. Used carelessly, they leak data, act on false information and create risks nobody signed off.

This certification gives managers, analysts and IT and operations professionals a clear, vendor-neutral understanding of how agents actually work, without needing to code. You will learn how large language models behave, how tools, retrieval and memory turn a model into an agent, how to pick and size the right use cases, how to secure and govern agents in a regulated Pakistani environment, and how to run them at scale with the right KPIs, costs and operating model.

Every session uses realistic cases from Pakistani banks, telecom operators and service firms, and ends with a scored test. The final exam is tough and scenario-based: passing it shows you can make sound decisions about agents, not just repeat definitions.
audience: Managers and department heads who must decide where AI agents should and should not be used
Business and data analysts who will design, test or evaluate agent use cases
IT, architecture and information security professionals who will integrate and secure agents
Operations, customer service and shared-services leaders planning automation programmes
Risk, compliance and audit staff who will oversee AI in regulated organisations
outcomes: Explain how large language models work at a practical level and what makes a system genuinely agentic
Describe the building blocks of an agent (tools, retrieval, memory, orchestration) and choose the right pattern for a task
Select, size and prioritise agent use cases using value, feasibility, data readiness and risk
Identify the main agent risks, including hallucination, prompt injection and data leakage, and apply practical controls
Design governance for agents that fits Pakistan's regulatory and privacy environment
Plan deployment and scaling: evaluation, monitoring, KPIs, cost control, operating model and upskilling

cards.title: From answering to acting
cards.body:
Most professionals in Pakistan first met generative AI as a chat window: you type a question, it writes an answer. That is useful, but the human still does all the work around it. You copy the answer into an email, check the customer record yourself, raise the ticket yourself.

An **AI agent** closes that gap. It is given a **goal** rather than a single question, and it is connected to the systems where work happens. It can decide which steps are needed, look things up, call a system, check the result and try again until the goal is met or it needs a human.

Think of the difference this way:

| | Chat assistant | AI agent |
|---|---|---|
| Input | A question | A goal |
| Output | Text for a human | Actions plus a report |
| Systems | None, or copy-paste | Connected through tools |
| Steps | One reply | Many steps in a loop |
| Who checks | The reader | Built-in checks plus people at set points |

This shift is why agents matter for business: they can take on whole slices of a process, not just help write about it. It is also why they need much stronger governance. A wrong sentence in a chat reply is embarrassing; a wrong action in a core banking or billing system can cost money, customers and regulatory standing.

In this course you will learn to judge agents the way a good manager judges a new team member: what can it do, what should it be allowed to do alone, how will we know it is doing well, and what happens when it gets something wrong.

cards.title: How a large language model actually works
cards.body:
At the heart of every agent is a **large language model (LLM)**. You do not need the mathematics, but you do need an accurate mental model.

**1. It works in tokens.** Text is split into small pieces called tokens: whole words, parts of words or punctuation. Roughly, a token is three to four characters of English. Urdu and Roman Urdu usually need more tokens for the same meaning, which affects cost and speed.

**2. It predicts the next token.** Given all the text so far, the model calculates how likely each possible next token is, picks one, adds it, and repeats. A long, fluent answer is built one token at a time.

**3. It learned patterns, not a database of facts.** During **pre-training** the model saw a vast amount of text and adjusted billions of internal numbers (parameters) to get better at prediction. Facts are stored only indirectly, as patterns. There is no table it looks up.

**4. It was then shaped to be helpful.** **Post-training** (instruction tuning and learning from human or AI feedback) teaches the model to follow instructions, use a conversational style, refuse harmful requests and, in newer models, reason step by step before answering.

The practical consequence: an LLM produces the **most plausible** continuation, which is usually but not always the **true** one. When it lacks the right information, it can still produce a confident, well-formatted, wrong answer. This is called **hallucination**, and it is a built-in property of how the model generates text, not a bug that will simply be patched away. Agents reduce it by giving the model real data to work from and by checking its outputs, which you will learn in Session 2.

cards.title: Five practical limits every manager should know
cards.body:
Five properties of LLMs shape every agent design decision.

- **Context window.** The model can only consider a limited amount of text at once: the instructions, the conversation, retrieved documents and tool results. Modern windows are large, but not infinite, and quality can drop when the important detail is buried in a very long context. Good agents feed the model only what it needs.
- **No memory between calls by default.** Each request is independent. Anything the model appears to remember was put back into the context by the application. Memory is a design feature, not a given.
- **Knowledge cutoff.** The model knows nothing after its training data ended, and nothing about your organisation's private data unless you supply it. It does not know today's policy rate, this morning's tariff change or your customer's balance.
- **Non-determinism.** The same prompt can produce different outputs. A setting often called **temperature** controls how much randomness is used when choosing tokens; lower values make outputs more consistent but never guarantee identical results across model versions or providers.
- **Weak at exact work without tools.** Precise arithmetic, counting, date calculations and lookups are unreliable when done in the model's head. Agents should hand these to tools: a calculator, a database query, a rules engine.

Keep these five in mind and many design choices become obvious. For example, a loan agent should never estimate an instalment amount itself; it should call the bank's approved calculation service and quote that result.

cards.title: Fluent is not the same as correct
cards.body: The most common mistake new users make is trusting an answer because it **sounds** expert. LLM output is always well written; that tells you nothing about accuracy. When reviewing any AI output, ask: **where did this fact come from?** If the answer is 'the model's general knowledge', treat specific numbers, names, dates, regulations and policy details as unverified until checked against a source system or document.

cards.question: A relationship manager asks a general-purpose chat model for the current profit rate on her bank's own term deposit product. It replies confidently with a specific figure. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: The figure is probably correct, because modern models are trained on large amounts of recent banking and financial data
The figure is correct only if the temperature setting was low
The figure is correct if the model gave the same answer twice in a row
It is unreliable: the model cannot see the bank's current rates unless they are supplied to it
cards.explanation: The model's knowledge comes from training data with a cutoff and does not include the bank's live internal rates. A low temperature or a repeated answer only makes output more consistent, not more true: a model can repeat the same hallucination.

cards.title: The agent loop
cards.body:
What makes a system **agentic** is not the model alone but the **loop** wrapped around it. A typical agent repeats four steps:

1. **Think / plan.** Given the goal and everything known so far, decide the next step. For example: 'I need the customer's last three bills before I can judge the dispute.'
2. **Act.** Call a tool: query the billing system, search the policy library, draft an email, create a ticket.
3. **Observe.** Read the result of the action and add it to the context.
4. **Decide.** Is the goal met? If yes, stop and report. If not, loop back to step 1. If stuck, out of budget or facing a risky step, hand over to a human.

This pattern is sometimes summarised as **reason and act**: the model alternates between reasoning about what to do and taking actions, using what each action returns to inform its next thought.

The loop is powerful because the agent can adapt. If the billing system returns an error, it can try a different query. If a document is missing, it can ask for it. A fixed script cannot do that.

The loop is also where risk lives. Every iteration costs money and time, and every action can change something real. Well-designed agents therefore have **stopping rules**: a maximum number of steps, a cost or time budget, a list of actions that always require approval, and clear conditions for escalation. An agent without stopping rules can loop endlessly, repeat a payment instruction, or keep emailing a customer. As Fleet Commander, you will always ask: what makes this agent stop?

cards.title: The five ingredients of an agentic system
cards.body:
Use these five ingredients as a checklist when someone calls a product an 'agent'.

| Ingredient | What it means | Business question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| **Goal** | A desired outcome, not just a single prompt | Who sets the goal, and how is success defined? |
| **Planning** | Breaking the goal into steps and choosing the order | Can it change plan when something fails? |
| **Tools** | Connections that let it read data or take actions | Which systems can it touch, with what permissions? |
| **Memory** | Information kept across steps or sessions | What does it remember, for how long, and who can see it? |
| **Loop** | Repeating act-observe-decide until done | What makes it stop or escalate? |

A system with all five is genuinely agentic. Many products have only some of them. A chatbot that answers from a fixed FAQ has none of planning, tools or loop. A robotic process automation (RPA) bot has tools and a loop but follows a fixed script with no model-based planning. A retrieval assistant that searches documents and answers has a tool but usually no goal beyond one answer.

Agency is therefore a **spectrum**, not a yes/no label. More agency brings more flexibility and more risk. The design question is never 'how agentic can we make it?' but 'how much agency does this task actually need?'. A surprising number of business problems are best solved with the least agentic option that works, which is a theme you will revisit in Session 2.

cards.title: Case: the bill dispute agent at a Lahore telecom operator
cards.body:
A mobile operator headquartered in Lahore receives about 40,000 billing complaints a month through its app and helpline. Most are simple: a customer believes a data bundle was charged twice or a call package did not activate.

The customer experience team, led by **Sana Iqbal**, pilots an agent with one goal: *resolve or correctly route each billing complaint within ten minutes*.

How the five ingredients appear:

- **Goal:** resolve or route the complaint, with a defined outcome code.
- **Planning:** the agent decides whether it needs usage records, bundle activation logs or recharge history, depending on the complaint.
- **Tools:** read-only access to usage and billing records; a tool to issue a credit, limited to PKR 500 per case; a ticketing tool to route to human agents.
- **Memory:** within the case, it keeps what it has already checked; across cases, it keeps nothing about the customer beyond the normal case record.
- **Loop and stopping rules:** maximum eight tool calls; any credit above PKR 500, any complaint mentioning fraud or SIM replacement, and any customer who asks for a human go straight to a person.

In the pilot, the agent resolved 58% of complaints end to end, routed most of the rest with a clear summary, and cut average handling time for routed cases because staff no longer had to gather records. Two problems appeared: it sometimes misread Roman Urdu messages that mixed bundle names with slang, and it once tried to issue two PKR 400 credits for the same complaint. The team added a rule that limits credits **per complaint**, not per tool call, which is exactly the kind of control you will design later in this course.

cards.question: Which system is the best example of a genuinely agentic system rather than an assistant or fixed automation?
options: A supplier onboarding system that picks the checks needed, queries registries, chases documents and escalates
A bot that copies values from emailed PDF forms into a fixed set of screens, following a recorded script step by step every time
A chat assistant that drafts a reply to a customer email when an officer pastes it in
A search tool that returns the five most relevant policy pages for a question
cards.explanation: Only the onboarding system has a goal, plans its own steps, uses several tools, and loops until done or escalates. The recorded-script bot has tools and repetition but no model-based planning; the drafting assistant and search tool each produce a single output for a human.

cards.title: Levels of autonomy: agreeing what the agent may do alone
cards.body:
Arguments about agents often happen because people picture different amounts of independence. A shared scale fixes that. In this course we use five levels.

| Level | Name | What the AI does | What the human does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | Assistant | Answers or drafts on request | Decides and does everything |
| **1** | Copilot | Prepares work inside the process (drafts, summaries, suggested actions) | Reviews and executes every action |
| **2** | Supervised agent | Plans and prepares actions; executes after approval | Approves each consequential action |
| **3** | Bounded autonomy | Executes on its own within set limits (amount, type, customer segment) | Handles exceptions and reviews samples |
| **4** | High autonomy | Executes broadly, sets its own sub-goals | Sets objectives and monitors outcomes |

Three principles for using the scale:

- **Autonomy is set per action, not per agent.** The same agent can read records at level 3 and move money at level 2.
- **Match autonomy to reversibility and impact.** Easily reversed, low-value actions can run with more autonomy; irreversible, high-value or customer-affecting actions need approval.
- **Earn autonomy with evidence.** Start lower, measure accuracy on real cases, then raise the level for specific actions when the data supports it. Lower it again if quality drops.

In regulated Pakistani sectors, almost all production agents today sit at levels 1 to 3. Level 4 is rare and is generally limited to low-risk internal tasks.

cards.title: Case: one agent, three autonomy levels in trade finance
cards.body:
The trade operations unit of a Karachi-based bank processes import letters of credit. Document checkers compare shipping documents (invoice, bill of lading, insurance certificate) against the terms of the credit, a slow, detail-heavy task.

**Kamran Siddiqui**, head of trade operations, sponsors an agent and agrees autonomy levels with risk management **per action**:

| Action | Autonomy level | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Extract data from scanned documents and fill the checklist | 3 | High volume, every field visible to the checker, easy to correct |
| Flag possible discrepancies with page references | 1 | The agent suggests; the checker decides |
| Draft the discrepancy notice to the presenting bank | 2 | Drafted by the agent, sent only after checker approval |
| Accept documents and release payment | Not delegated | Remains a human decision with existing dual control |

After three months, extraction accuracy on key fields was 97% on a sample checked by staff, and checkers spent their time on judgement rather than typing. The team then proposed moving the discrepancy flags for a few simple, objective checks (for example, matching amounts and dates) from level 1 to level 2, supported by the accuracy data.

The lesson: autonomy is not a single switch. Breaking a process into actions lets you capture value quickly where risk is low while keeping firm human control where it matters.

cards.title: Test claims of 'fully autonomous' agents
cards.body:
Vendors often label any AI feature an 'agent'. Before you believe it, ask four questions:

- **Which tools can it call**, and can I see the list?
- **Who decides the steps**: the model, or a fixed script?
- **What stops it**: step limits, budgets, approval points?
- **What did it get wrong in testing**, and how was that measured?

If the vendor cannot answer the last question with data from cases like yours, you are looking at a demo, not a deployable agent.

cards.question: An insurance company's claims agent currently drafts settlement decisions that an officer approves. Over six months it has been reliable on small motor claims. What is the soundest next step on the autonomy scale?
options: Move the whole claims agent to level 4 so it can settle all claim types alone, given its six-month track record
Keep everything at level 2 permanently, because claims always affect customers
Move the agent to level 0 until regulators publish AI-specific claims rules
Move only small, defined motor claims within a value limit to level 3, with sampling and rollback
cards.explanation: Autonomy should be raised per action and backed by evidence, within limits, with monitoring. Jumping the whole agent to level 4 ignores risk differences between claim types; freezing at level 2 forever ignores the evidence and the value it could release.

cards.title: Launch Bay take-aways
items: An LLM predicts the most plausible next token; plausible is usually, but not always, true, so hallucination is built in.
Context window, no default memory, knowledge cutoff, non-determinism and weak exact calculation shape every agent design.
An agent pursues a goal by looping through plan, act, observe and decide, using tools to reach real systems.
Goal, planning, tools, memory and loop are the five ingredients; agency is a spectrum, not a label.
Set autonomy per action, matched to impact and reversibility, and raise it only with evidence.
Every agent needs stopping rules: step limits, budgets, approval points and escalation triggers.

cards.prompt: Pick one process in your department. Break it into four or five actions and, for each one, decide which autonomy level (0 to 4) you would be comfortable with today and what evidence would make you raise it.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes how a large language model generates an answer?
options: It searches an internal database of verified facts and formats the best match
It runs a fixed set of rules written by its developers for each topic
It repeatedly predicts a likely next token based on the text so far
It copies the closest matching passage from its training documents
quiz.explanation: An LLM builds output one token at a time by predicting likely continuations. It has no table of verified facts to look up, which is why plausible but false answers (hallucinations) can occur. It does not simply retrieve stored passages either.

quiz.question: A team notices that their customer-service model gives slightly different wording for the same question each time. A manager wants identical outputs for audit reasons. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Lower temperature improves consistency, but the design should log each actual output rather than rely on reproducing it
Setting temperature to zero guarantees exactly the same output forever, even after the provider updates or replaces the underlying model
The variation means the model is faulty and should be replaced
Variation only happens with Urdu input, so forcing English will solve it
quiz.explanation: Lower temperature reduces randomness, but it does not guarantee identical results across model versions or infrastructure changes. For audit, the reliable control is to log the actual inputs and outputs. Variation is normal behaviour, not a fault, and is not language-specific.

quiz.question: Why does a chat model appear to remember what you said earlier in the same conversation?
options: Each message permanently updates the model's internal parameters so it learns the conversation as it goes
The model stores a private profile of each user on its servers by default
Earlier messages are cached in the model's training data for reuse
The application re-sends the earlier conversation to the model as context on every call
quiz.explanation: Models are stateless between calls. The application re-sends prior conversation (or a summary) in the context window. Conversations do not retrain the model's parameters, and any long-term memory is a separate feature built by the application.

quiz.question: A finance analyst at a Faisalabad textile group asks an agent to calculate the PKR equivalent of 27 import invoices at each invoice date's exchange rate. Which design is most reliable?
options: Let the model do the conversions itself, since modern models are good at arithmetic
Give the agent tools to fetch each date's approved rate and to calculate, and report the tool results
Paste all 27 invoices into one prompt and ask the model to carefully re-check its own arithmetic before answering
Ask the model to estimate the average rate for the period and apply it to all invoices
quiz.explanation: Exact lookups and arithmetic should be delegated to tools: an approved rate source and a calculator. Self-checking by the same model can repeat errors, and an average rate gives a wrong answer by design.

quiz.question: Which feature most clearly separates an AI agent from a standard chat assistant?
options: It writes longer and more detailed answers
It runs on a larger, more recent language model with a bigger context window and better reasoning
It pursues a goal through repeated cycles of planning, acting with tools and observing results
It is available on mobile apps and messaging platforms
quiz.explanation: The defining feature is the goal-directed loop with tools. Answer length, model size and delivery channel do not make a system agentic.

quiz.question: An HR agent at a Rawalpindi services firm keeps calling the leave system repeatedly when the system returns an error, running up cost overnight. Which missing design element is the main cause?
options: A larger context window so the agent can hold more of the error messages
Stopping rules such as a maximum number of steps, a budget and an escalation path
Long-term memory of each employee's leave history so it can skip the leave system call entirely
A more detailed system prompt describing the company's culture
quiz.explanation: Runaway loops are prevented by stopping rules: step limits, cost or time budgets, and escalation when stuck. A larger context window or more memory would not stop the loop, and a culture description is irrelevant to the failure.

quiz.question: A vendor demonstrates an 'autonomous agent' for accounts payable. On inspection, it follows the same recorded sequence of screens for every invoice and fails if a field moves. How should you classify it?
options: Scripted automation with tools and repetition but no model-based planning, so not genuinely agentic
A level 4 agent, because it works without human input
A level 2 supervised agent, because it handles invoices
A retrieval assistant, because it reads invoice data
quiz.explanation: A fixed recorded sequence that cannot adapt is classic scripted automation. Working without human input does not make it agentic; the missing ingredient is planning that adapts to the situation.

quiz.question: Under the course's five-level autonomy scale, an agent that prepares a funds transfer and executes it only after an officer clicks approve is operating at which level for that action?
options: Level 0: assistant
Level 1: copilot
Level 3: bounded autonomy
Level 2: supervised agent
quiz.explanation: The agent plans and prepares the action and executes it after explicit human approval, which is level 2. At level 1 the human executes the action; at level 3 the agent executes alone within limits.

quiz.question: A microfinance bank in Multan wants one agent that can (a) look up a borrower's repayment history, (b) send payment reminders by SMS and (c) reschedule loans. How should autonomy be set?
options: One level for the whole agent, set by its riskiest action, so every one of the three actions needs approval
Per action: high for read-only look-ups, bounded for templated reminders, approval for rescheduling
One level for the whole agent, set by its most common action, so all three run autonomously
Autonomy should not be set until the agent has run in production for a year
quiz.explanation: Autonomy is best set per action according to impact and reversibility. Rescheduling changes a contract and needs approval; look-ups are low-risk. One level for everything either wastes value or creates unnecessary risk.

quiz.question: A bank's policy chatbot answers staff questions accurately about policies issued last year but confidently gives outdated guidance about a circular issued last month. No documents are connected to it. What is the most likely cause?
options: The temperature is set too high
The context window is too small for the question
The model's knowledge comes from training data with a cutoff and it has no access to the new circular
The model has been deliberately trained to ignore regulatory updates
quiz.explanation: Without connected documents, the model relies on what it learned in training, which stops at a cutoff and excludes private or recent material. Temperature affects randomness, not knowledge, and a short question does not strain the context window.

sessions.title: Anatomy of an Agent
sessions.summary: Open the hood: how agents call tools, ground answers in your documents, remember, and coordinate with other agents and people, and how to evaluate whether any of it works.
objectives: Explain how function calling lets a model use business systems without executing anything itself
Describe the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline and its common failure points
Distinguish short-term, long-term and shared memory and their governance implications
Choose between a fixed workflow, a single agent, multiple agents and human-in-the-loop designs
Design an evaluation approach that measures both final answers and the steps taken

cards.title: The parts of an agent
cards.body:
Every agent, whichever vendor or framework it comes from, is assembled from the same parts. Learn these and you can read any architecture diagram.

| Part | Role | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **Model** | Reasons, plans and writes | The officer's judgement |
| **Instructions** (system prompt) | Role, rules, tone, limits | The job description and SOPs |
| **Tools** | Read data and take actions in systems | System access rights |
| **Knowledge** (retrieval) | Finds relevant documents and records | The policy library |
| **Memory** | Keeps information across steps or sessions | Case notes and file history |
| **Orchestration** | Runs the loop, routes work, manages hand-offs | The supervisor and workflow |
| **Guardrails** | Checks inputs, outputs and actions against rules | Maker-checker and compliance review |
| **Logging and evaluation** | Records what happened and measures quality | Audit trail and QA |

Two points matter for managers.

First, **the model is only one part**. Most failures in production come from the other parts: a tool that returns confusing errors, a document library full of outdated versions, missing guardrails, or no logs to explain what happened. Swapping to a bigger model rarely fixes those.

Second, **the parts are separable**. You can change the model while keeping the tools and guardrails, or tighten guardrails without touching the model. Designs that keep these parts loosely coupled are easier to govern, test and move between providers, which matters for vendor risk and for data residency decisions you will meet in Session 4.

cards.title: Tools and function calling
cards.body:
A model cannot press buttons. It can only produce text. **Function calling** (also called tool use) is the mechanism that turns text into action safely.

How it works:

1. The application tells the model which tools exist, each with a **name**, a **description** and the **parameters** it accepts, for example `get_account_balance(account_id)` or `create_ticket(category, priority, summary)`.
2. When the model decides a tool is needed, it replies with a **structured request**: the tool name and argument values.
3. The **application**, not the model, checks that request and executes it using its own credentials and permissions.
4. The result is sent back to the model, which continues its reasoning.

This separation is the single most important control point in agent design. Because your code sits between the model's request and the real system, you can validate arguments, enforce limits, require approval, and log every call. If a model asks to refund PKR 50,000 when the tool's limit is PKR 5,000, the application refuses, whatever the model 'thinks'.

Tools come in two broad kinds:

- **Read tools** fetch information (look up a customer, search a policy). Lower risk, but they can still expose data.
- **Write tools** change something (send a message, update a record, move money). Higher risk; these carry approvals and limits.

Industry has also converged on **open protocols** for connecting tools, such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), so one integration can serve many agents. Standard connectors speed things up, but every connected tool still needs the same access review as any other system integration.

Tool **descriptions** matter more than people expect: the model chooses tools based on them. Vague descriptions lead to wrong tool choices.

cards.title: Give agents narrow tools, not master keys
cards.body: A common shortcut is to give an agent one powerful tool, such as 'run any database query' or 'call any API'. Resist it. Build **narrow, purpose-specific tools** with limits baked in: `issue_bundle_credit(customer_id, amount)` capped at PKR 500, rather than general write access to the billing database. Narrow tools are easier for the model to use correctly, easier to test and much easier to defend in an audit.

cards.question: An agent decides it needs to block a customer's debit card and produces a request to call the block_card tool. Who actually executes the block?
options: The application layer, which can validate, check permissions and log the request first
The language model, directly inside the card system
The customer, who must confirm on the mobile app every time
The model provider's servers, which log in to the card system using the bank's stored passwords
cards.explanation: In function calling the model only proposes a structured call. The application executes it with its own credentials, which is why validation, limits, approvals and logging are enforced there. The model never directly touches the card system.

cards.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
cards.body:
Models do not know your policies, products or customers. **Retrieval-augmented generation** fixes this by finding relevant material at the moment of the question and placing it in the context, so the model answers from **your** sources rather than from memory.

The pipeline has two halves.

**Preparing the knowledge (done in advance):**

1. **Collect** approved sources: policy manuals, product sheets, circulars, FAQs.
2. **Split** them into chunks, such as sections or paragraphs.
3. **Index** each chunk, usually by converting it into an **embedding**, a list of numbers that captures meaning, so that similar meanings sit close together. Many systems also keep a keyword index.

**Answering (at question time):**

4. **Retrieve** the chunks most relevant to the question, combining meaning-based and keyword search, and ideally filtering by the user's access rights.
5. **Generate** an answer using only those chunks, with **citations** back to the source.

Where RAG goes wrong:

- **Stale or conflicting sources:** old and new versions of a circular both indexed.
- **Poor chunking:** a table split in half, or a rule separated from its exception.
- **Retrieval misses:** the right passage exists but is not found, often with acronyms, Urdu terms or scanned PDFs.
- **Permission leaks:** the index ignores who is allowed to see which document.
- **Ungrounded answers:** the model adds detail not in the retrieved text.

The lesson: RAG quality is mostly a **content management** problem. Document ownership, version control and access rules matter as much as the model.

cards.title: Case: the branch policy assistant in Islamabad
cards.body:
A mid-sized bank with 300 branches launches a policy assistant for branch staff. **Ayesha Raza**, from the operations policy team, owns the project. The goal: answer questions like 'what documents do I need to open an account for a minor?' with citations, so staff stop phoning head office.

The first version is indexed on the shared drive. Within two weeks, problems appear:

- A teller in Peshawar gets an answer based on a **superseded** account-opening SOP, because both versions were on the drive.
- Questions using local terms, for example asking about 'B-form' rather than the formal name of the child registration certificate, retrieve nothing useful.
- Several key circulars are **scanned images**, so their text was never indexed.
- One answer cites an internal audit memo that branch staff should not see.

Ayesha's fixes are mostly not technical:

- Only documents with an owner, a version number and an 'in force' status are indexed; superseded versions are removed automatically.
- A **glossary** maps common local terms and abbreviations to formal names.
- Scanned documents are run through text recognition and spot-checked.
- The index stores each document's **audience**, and retrieval filters by the user's role.
- The assistant must cite its source and say 'I could not find this in current policy' when retrieval is weak, rather than guessing.

After the changes, a sample review of 400 answers found 94% correct and properly cited, and calls to the head-office helpdesk fell by about a third. The model was never changed.

cards.title: Memory: what the agent keeps, and why it is a governance issue
cards.body:
Because models are stateless, everything an agent 'remembers' is a design choice. There are three useful layers.

- **Working (short-term) memory:** what is in the context for the current task, such as the goal, steps taken and tool results. It disappears when the task ends. Long tasks may need **summarising** to stay within the context window, and summaries can lose details.
- **Long-term memory:** information stored outside the model and retrieved later, such as a customer's stated preferences, previous case outcomes or lessons from past tasks. It works like retrieval over the agent's own notes.
- **Shared memory:** a common workspace or record that several agents or people read and write, such as a case file that a triage agent, a specialist agent and a human officer all update.

Memory makes agents more useful: customers do not repeat themselves, and agents improve with experience. It also creates **governance obligations**:

- **Personal data:** remembered details about customers or employees are personal data. You need a purpose, a retention period and a way to correct or delete it.
- **Contamination:** a wrong fact written to memory, or an instruction planted by an attacker, can be reused in many later tasks.
- **Access:** memory from one customer or department must never surface in another's session.

A sound rule: **remember the minimum needed for the purpose, for the shortest sensible time, in a place you can inspect.** Prefer storing structured facts in the system of record over free-text 'memories' that nobody reviews.

cards.question: A telecom's sales agent stores free-text notes about each customer conversation in long-term memory to personalise future offers. Which risk is the most important to address first?
options: The notes will make responses noticeably slower as memory grows, frustrating customers on busy days
The notes might make the agent too polite
The notes will cause the model's parameters to change over time
They are personal data needing a purpose, retention limit, access control and correction route
cards.explanation: Remembered customer details are personal data and must be governed: purpose, retention, access and correction. Speed and tone are minor issues, and stored notes do not retrain the model's parameters; they are retrieved into context.

cards.title: Workflows versus agents
cards.body:
Not every AI system should be an agent. A key design choice is **who decides the path**.

- In a **workflow**, the steps are fixed in advance by designers. The model is used inside specific steps, for example 'classify this email', then 'extract these fields', then 'draft a reply', but the sequence is set by code. Workflows are predictable, cheaper, easier to test and easier to explain to auditors.
- In an **agent**, the model decides the next step at run time. It is flexible and handles variety, but it is less predictable, costs more per task and is harder to test exhaustively.

A practical rule: **use the simplest design that meets the need.** Start with a single model call with good retrieval. If the task has stable, known steps, build a workflow. Reach for an agent only when the path genuinely varies from case to case and cannot be mapped in advance.

| Situation | Better fit |
|---|---|
| Same steps every time, high volume, strict audit | Workflow |
| A few known case types, each with its own steps | Workflow with routing |
| Open-ended investigation, unpredictable data needs | Agent |
| Mostly standard with occasional odd cases | Workflow, with an agent or human for exceptions |

Many successful deployments are **hybrids**: a predictable workflow handles the main path, and an agent is called only for the messy exceptions, inside tight limits. This gives most of the flexibility with much less risk.

cards.title: Orchestration patterns
cards.body:
When a task needs more than one model call, a small set of patterns covers most designs.

- **Chaining:** output of step one feeds step two (extract, then validate, then draft). Simple and testable.
- **Routing:** a classifier sends each request to the right specialised path, for example billing, technical or sales.
- **Parallel work:** several calls run at once, such as checking a contract against five policy areas simultaneously, then combining results.
- **Orchestrator and workers:** a lead agent breaks a task into sub-tasks, assigns them to worker agents and assembles the result. Useful when sub-tasks are not known in advance.
- **Generator and checker:** one call produces work and another reviews it against criteria, looping until it passes or a limit is reached.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** defined points where a person approves, corrects or takes over. Not a fallback; a designed step.

**Multi-agent systems** combine several agents with different roles, tools and permissions. Benefits: each agent has a narrow job and narrow access, and specialists can be tested separately. Costs: more model calls, more hand-offs where context can be lost, and harder debugging when agents pass errors to each other.

Two design rules: give each agent **only the tools its role needs**, and make sure every hand-off includes enough context and an audit record. If you cannot explain which agent did what, you cannot govern the system.

cards.title: Case: redesigning employee onboarding at a telecom
cards.body:
The HR shared-services team of a telecom operator in Islamabad onboards around 150 staff a month across Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad. **Faisal Ahmed**, HR operations lead, first asks for 'a multi-agent system' after seeing a vendor demo.

The architecture review asks: does the path really vary? Mapping 60 recent cases shows that 85% follow the same steps: verify documents, create the employee record, request laptop and access, schedule induction, send the welcome pack. The remaining 15% involve odd cases: contractors converting to permanent, staff transferring from a group company, missing degree verification.

The final design is a **hybrid**:

- A **workflow** handles the standard path. A model extracts data from CNIC copies, degrees and offer letters; rules check completeness; tools create records and tickets in a fixed order.
- An **exceptions agent** is invoked only when rules flag an unusual case. It can read the HR record, the offer letter and policy documents, and drafts a recommended path for an HR officer to approve (autonomy level 2).
- **Human checkpoints:** an HR officer approves the employee record before payroll set-up, and IT security approves any access beyond the role's standard profile.

Results after the first quarter: standard onboarding time fell from nine working days to four, and HR officers spent most of their time on the exception cases that needed judgement. The workflow part was cheap to run and easy to audit; the agent's cost was limited because it handled only a small share of cases. The multi-agent design from the demo would have cost more and been harder to test, with little extra benefit.

cards.question: A bank's account-closure process follows the same eight steps for every request, must be fully auditable, and runs 2,000 times a month. Which design fits best?
options: A fully autonomous agent that decides the steps for each closure
A multi-agent system with a separate agent for each of the eight steps, coordinating freely to find faster paths
A defined workflow, using a model only in steps needing language understanding, exceptions to people
No AI at all, because regulated processes cannot use models
cards.explanation: Fixed steps, high volume and strict audit point to a workflow, using a model only where it adds value. Agent-led designs add cost and unpredictability without benefit here. Regulated processes can use AI with proper controls.

cards.title: Evaluating agents: outcomes and trajectories
cards.body:
You cannot manage what you do not measure, and agents are harder to measure than traditional software because their output varies. A sound evaluation approach has four layers.

**1. A test set before you build.** Collect a representative set of real cases with the correct outcome agreed by experts: typical cases, hard cases, edge cases and cases where the right answer is to escalate. Include Urdu, Roman Urdu and poor-quality inputs if real users send them. A few hundred well-chosen cases beats thousands of easy ones.

**2. Outcome metrics.** Did the agent reach the right final result? Examples: task success rate, accuracy of extracted fields, correct escalation rate, groundedness (claims supported by cited sources).

**3. Trajectory metrics.** Did it get there the right way? An agent can reach a correct answer by luck or through unsafe steps. Check whether it called the right tools, in a sensible order, without unnecessary or forbidden actions, within step and cost limits.

**4. Reviewers.** Use a mix of automated checks (exact match, rules), **model-based grading** (a model scoring outputs against a rubric, which is fast but must itself be checked against human judgement), and **human expert review** on samples, especially for high-risk outputs.

Run the full test set **every time** something changes: the model, the prompt, a tool, or the documents. Changes that improve one area often quietly break another; this regression testing is your safety net. Finally, remember that offline tests are not enough. Production monitoring, covered in Session 5, catches what test sets missed.

cards.title: Write the exam before you build the agent
cards.body: Agree the evaluation set and the pass criteria with the business owner **before** development starts, for example 'at least 95% of fields correct, 100% of fraud-related cases escalated, no write action outside limits'. This prevents endless debate later about whether the agent is 'good enough', and stops teams from tuning the agent to a few impressive demos.

cards.title: Engine Deck take-aways
items: An agent is model plus instructions, tools, knowledge, memory, orchestration, guardrails and logging; most failures come from the parts around the model.
In function calling the model only proposes; the application validates and executes, making it the key control point.
RAG grounds answers in your documents; its quality depends on version control, chunking, access filtering and citations.
Memory is a design choice with privacy obligations: minimum data, limited retention, inspectable storage.
Use the simplest design that works: workflows for stable paths, agents for genuinely variable ones, hybrids for both.
Evaluate both outcomes and trajectories, on a test set agreed before building, and re-run it after every change.

cards.prompt: Think of an AI tool or proposal in your organisation. Which of its parts (model, tools, knowledge, memory, orchestration, guardrails, logging) is weakest today, and what would you fix first?

quiz.question: In function calling, what does the language model itself produce when it decides to use a tool?
options: A structured request naming the tool and arguments, which the application validates and runs
A direct connection to the target system using its own credentials
A compiled program that the provider's server runs immediately against the target system without further checks
A message to the end user asking them to run the tool manually
quiz.explanation: The model outputs a structured tool request; the surrounding application decides whether and how to execute it. The model holds no credentials and has no direct connection to systems.

quiz.question: An agent in a Karachi insurance company repeatedly chooses the 'search_claims' tool when it should use 'search_policies'. Both tools work correctly when called. What should the team look at first?
options: Increase the model's context window so it can consider both tools' documentation at once
Add long-term memory of past tool choices
Replace the model with a larger one
The tool names and descriptions, which the model relies on to choose between tools
quiz.explanation: Models choose tools from their names and descriptions; vague or overlapping descriptions cause wrong choices. Upgrading the model or adding memory may not help, and context size is unrelated to the confusion.

quiz.question: In a retrieval-augmented generation system, what is the main purpose of converting document chunks into embeddings?
options: To compress documents so they take less disk space
To allow searching by meaning, so passages with similar meaning to the question can be found even without the same words
To encrypt documents so the model cannot read them
To translate all documents into English
quiz.explanation: Embeddings represent meaning as numbers, enabling semantic search. They are not a compression, encryption or translation mechanism, although many systems combine them with keyword search.

quiz.question: A bank's policy assistant gives a branch officer in Quetta an answer based on a circular that was replaced six months ago. Both versions are in the index. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: Instruct the model in its system prompt to always prefer the more recent document whenever two sources conflict
Increase the number of chunks retrieved per question
Index only documents with an owner and an in-force status, removing superseded versions automatically
Switch to a model with a more recent training cutoff
quiz.explanation: The root cause is content governance: superseded documents should not be in the index. Prompting the model to prefer newer documents is unreliable, retrieving more chunks may bring in even more conflicts, and the model's training cutoff is irrelevant to private circulars.

quiz.question: An HR knowledge assistant correctly answers most questions but once quoted salary bands from a confidential compensation document to a junior employee. What is the most important control missing?
options: A citation requirement for every answer
A lower temperature setting
A larger, more capable embedding model to improve search quality across all HR documents
Retrieval filtered by the user's access rights to each document
quiz.explanation: The failure is a permission leak: retrieval ignored who may see which document. Citations would only show where the leak came from, while temperature and search quality do not enforce access.

quiz.question: Which situation is the strongest case for using an agent rather than a fixed workflow?
options: Investigating unusual corporate payment patterns, where the data needed depends on what each finding reveals
Sending monthly e-statements to all retail customers
Extracting the same ten fields from standard utility bills
Routing incoming emails into four fixed categories
quiz.explanation: Agents earn their extra cost and unpredictability when the path genuinely varies case by case, as in an open-ended investigation. The other tasks have stable steps that a workflow handles more cheaply and auditably.

quiz.question: A team builds a 'generator and checker' design for credit memo drafting. The checker is the same model with the instruction 'review the memo above'. Pilot results show the checker rarely catches factual errors. What is the best improvement?
options: Remove the checker, since model reviews are never useful
Run the same checker three times on every memo and accept the memo only if a majority of runs approve it
Give the checker explicit criteria and source-data tools, and calibrate it against human reviewers
Ask the generator to be more careful in its instructions
quiz.explanation: A checker needs explicit criteria, independent evidence to check against, and calibration against human judgement. Repeating a vague check repeats the same blind spots, and model-based review can be useful when designed properly.

quiz.question: A customer-service agent gives the correct final answer in a test case, but the log shows it called the refund tool, reversed the refund and then answered. How should this case be scored?
options: Pass, because the final answer was correct
Fail on trajectory, because it took an unnecessary and risky action even though the outcome was right
Pass, as long as the refund was reversed within one minute
Exclude the case from the test set as an outlier
quiz.explanation: Evaluation must cover trajectories as well as outcomes. An unnecessary write action is a real risk in production even if reversed. Excluding or passing such a case hides a serious defect.

quiz.question: A telecom proposes three agents: a triage agent, a billing agent and a retention agent that can offer discounts. Which access design is most appropriate?
options: All three share one service account with full CRM and billing access, which simplifies integration and logging
The triage agent holds all permissions and passes them to others as needed
Each agent gets read access to everything but write access to nothing
Each agent gets only the tools its role needs, with limits on billing adjustments and discount bands
quiz.explanation: Multi-agent designs should use narrow, role-specific tools and limits. A shared all-powerful account removes the security benefit of separation, and blanket read-only access would stop billing and retention agents from doing their jobs.

quiz.question: After a provider updates the underlying model, a bank's document agent seems fine in a quick demo. What should happen before the update reaches production?
options: Re-run the full agreed evaluation set and compare results with the previous version
Nothing; provider updates only improve quality
Ask three experienced staff members to try it for an afternoon and confirm it still feels right
Check that the response time is unchanged
quiz.explanation: Any change to model, prompt, tools or documents should trigger the full regression test, because improvements in one area can break another. A demo or informal trial covers too few cases, and speed is only one dimension.

sessions.title: Finding and Designing Agent Use Cases
sessions.summary: Choose the missions worth flying: screen processes for agent fit, score value, feasibility and risk, build an honest business case, check data readiness, decide build or buy, and run a pilot that produces real evidence.
objectives: Screen business processes for agent suitability using clear criteria
Prioritise a portfolio of use cases by value, feasibility and risk
Build a realistic business case with baseline, benefits, running costs and payback
Assess data readiness and choose between building, buying and configuring
Design a pilot with success criteria and exit rules agreed in advance

cards.title: Start with the work, not the technology
cards.body:
The weakest AI programmes begin with 'we need an agent strategy' and then look for somewhere to put agents. The strongest begin with **work that hurts**: long turnaround times, backlogs, error-prone manual checks, staff spending hours gathering information before they can make a decision.

A useful starting exercise is a **process walk**. Pick a process and follow one real case from start to finish, noting for each step:

- **What the person does** (read, look up, compare, decide, write, key in, chase).
- **Which systems and documents** they use.
- **How long it takes** and how long the case waits between steps.
- **What goes wrong** and how errors are found.

You will usually find that the decision itself takes minutes, while the surrounding work of finding, reading, reconciling and writing takes hours. That surrounding work is where agents shine.

Also look for **waiting time**. In many Pakistani organisations, a loan, claim or vendor payment spends most of its life waiting in someone's queue for a signature or a missing document. An agent that only speeds up the work step will not help if the case still waits three days for approval. Sometimes the right fix is a simpler process, not AI.

Finally, separate **task automation** from **process redesign**. Adding an agent to a broken process gives you a faster broken process. The biggest gains come when the process is redesigned around what agents and people each do best: agents gather, check and draft; people judge, approve and handle relationships.

cards.title: Screening: what makes a good agent candidate
cards.body:
Use a quick screen before any detailed analysis. Good candidates usually show most of these signs:

| Sign | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Volume and repetition** | Enough cases to repay the investment and to measure quality |
| **Language-heavy work** | Reading emails, documents, chats and writing responses is where models add most |
| **Variety that rules cannot handle** | If simple rules or RPA could do it, use them instead |
| **Accessible data and systems** | The agent needs tools: APIs, databases or at least structured exports |
| **Detectable, reversible errors** | Mistakes can be caught by checks or review and undone |
| **Known right answers** | Experts can say what good looks like, so you can evaluate |
| **A business owner** | Someone accountable for outcomes, not only IT |

Warning signs:

- **Rare, high-stakes, irreversible decisions** such as large credit approvals or employee terminations. Agents may assist, but should not decide.
- **No ground truth**: nobody can agree on the right answer, so you cannot test.
- **Data locked in paper or in systems with no integration route.**
- **Heavy regulatory constraints** that require a named human decision-maker with documented reasoning.
- **Tasks where the main value is the human relationship**, for example difficult conversations with key corporate clients.

A process does not have to pass every sign. But if it fails on data access, ground truth or reversibility, fix that first or choose a lower autonomy level, such as a copilot that drafts while people decide.

cards.title: Prioritising the portfolio: value, feasibility, risk
cards.body:
Most organisations end up with a long list of ideas. Score each candidate on three dimensions, from 1 (low) to 5 (high).

**Value**
- Hours of work released, turnaround improvement, revenue protected or gained, error and loss reduction, customer or employee experience.

**Feasibility**
- Data and system access, quality of documents, clarity of rules and right answers, availability of a business owner and subject-matter experts, technical complexity.

**Risk** (score high = risky)
- Customer and financial impact of errors, regulatory sensitivity, personal or confidential data involved, reversibility, reputational exposure.

Then place ideas into four groups:

- **Quick wins:** high value, high feasibility, low-to-moderate risk. Start here.
- **Strategic bets:** high value but harder or riskier. Plan carefully, often starting at a low autonomy level.
- **Fillers:** easy but low value. Do only if they build skills or reusable components.
- **Avoid for now:** low value and hard, or risk out of proportion to value.

Two refinements improve decisions:

- **Reuse:** favour use cases that build shared assets, such as a clean policy index, a customer-lookup tool or an evaluation framework, which later use cases can reuse.
- **Learning value:** your first one or two use cases should teach the organisation how to run agents safely. A visible, moderate-risk internal use case is often better than a high-profile customer-facing one.

cards.title: Case: scoring five ideas at a Lahore bank
cards.body:
The digital transformation office of a bank headquartered in Lahore collects 23 ideas from business units. **Usman Tariq**, the programme lead, shortlists five and runs a scoring workshop with business, IT, risk and compliance.

| Idea | Value | Feasibility | Risk | Group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Draft replies to customer service emails for agent review | 4 | 4 | 2 | Quick win |
| Pre-check SME loan files for missing documents | 4 | 3 | 2 | Quick win |
| Autonomous approval of personal loans up to PKR 1 million | 5 | 2 | 5 | Avoid for now |
| Investigation assistant for transaction monitoring alerts | 5 | 2 | 4 | Strategic bet |
| Summarise internal meeting minutes | 2 | 5 | 1 | Filler |

Decisions and reasoning:

- **Customer email drafting** goes first: high volume, staff remain in control (level 1), and errors are caught before sending.
- **SME loan pre-checks** follow, reusing the document extraction built for emails and a policy index.
- The **loan approval** idea is rejected for now. Credit decisions carry regulatory expectations of accountable human judgement and fair treatment, and the bank lacks clean data to evaluate fairness.
- The **alert investigation assistant** is planned as a strategic bet starting at level 1: it gathers transaction history, customer profile and adverse media for the analyst but never closes alerts itself.
- **Meeting summaries** are allowed as a self-service tool but not funded as a project.

The result is a portfolio, not a single bet: two quick wins to build credibility and reusable components, one strategic bet with careful controls, and clear reasons recorded for what was not done.

cards.question: Which candidate is the best first agent use case for an organisation with no prior agent deployments?
options: An agent that independently decides on employee disciplinary cases
An agent that approves high-value corporate payments overnight so that treasury staff do not need to work late
Drafting replies to IT helpdesk tickets for staff review, with good ticket history and an owner
An agent for a process that runs twice a year with no documented right answers
cards.explanation: The helpdesk drafting case has volume, data, a clear owner, reversible errors and human review, making it a good learning first step. Disciplinary decisions and large payments are high-stakes, and a twice-yearly process with no ground truth cannot be evaluated.

cards.title: Building an honest business case
cards.body:
Agent business cases fail when they count every minute saved as cash and ignore running costs. Build yours in five steps.

**1. Baseline.** Measure today: volume per month, handling time per case, error rate, turnaround, cost per staff hour (salary plus benefits and overheads, often called the loaded cost).

**2. Realistic scope.** Not every case is eligible. Estimate the share the agent can handle and how much time it saves on each, using pilot data where possible.

**3. Benefits.** Calculate hours released, then be honest about how they turn into value:
- **Cost avoided:** hiring you no longer need as volume grows.
- **Capacity redeployed:** staff move to higher-value work such as sales or complex cases. Value is real only if that work happens.
- **Quality and speed:** fewer errors, losses and complaints, faster turnaround that wins business.

**4. Full costs.**
- **One-time:** design, integration, data clean-up, evaluation, security review, training.
- **Running:** model usage (charged by tokens), platform and hosting, monitoring, human review of samples and exceptions, maintenance when systems or policies change, and periodic re-evaluation.

**5. Adoption curve.** Benefits ramp up over months as volume moves onto the agent and staff trust grows. Year one rarely delivers the full run rate.

Present a range (cautious, expected, optimistic) rather than one number, and state your assumptions. Risk and compliance colleagues will trust a case that admits uncertainty far more than one that promises a 400% return.

cards.title: Case: the numbers behind a customer email agent
cards.body:
**Hina Malik**, customer service head at a bank, prepares a business case for an agent that drafts replies to customer emails for staff to review and send.

**Baseline:** 30,000 emails per month, average handling time 9 minutes, loaded staff cost PKR 1,200 per hour.

**Pilot evidence:** 70% of emails are eligible (the rest are complaints needing investigation or unusual requests). For eligible emails, handling time falls from 9 to 4 minutes, a saving of 5 minutes.

**Monthly hours released:** 30,000 x 70% x 5 minutes = 105,000 minutes = **1,750 hours**, worth about **PKR 2.1 million** at PKR 1,200 per hour.

**Monthly running costs (estimated):**

| Item | PKR |
|---|---|
| Model usage | 350,000 |
| Platform, hosting and monitoring | 400,000 |
| Quality review analyst | 300,000 |
| **Total** | **1,050,000** |

**Net monthly benefit:** PKR 2.1 million minus PKR 1.05 million = **PKR 1.05 million**.

**One-time cost:** PKR 15 million, so simple payback is about **14 to 15 months** at full run rate, longer once the adoption ramp is included.

Hina's case is credible because she is explicit about how hours become value. Email volume is growing about 20% a year, so the bank avoids hiring around ten additional staff, and two current staff move to a new complaint-resolution team. She does not claim headcount cuts she cannot deliver. She also includes a quality benefit she cannot fully price: faster first responses, which the bank tracks through complaint escalations.

cards.question: An agent will handle 50% of 12,000 monthly cases, saving 6 minutes on each. Loaded staff cost is PKR 1,000 per hour, running costs are PKR 250,000 a month and one-time cost is PKR 4.2 million. What is the simple payback at full run rate?
options: 7 months
17 months
24 months
12 months
cards.explanation: Hours released: 12,000 x 50% x 6 minutes = 36,000 minutes = 600 hours, worth PKR 600,000. Net benefit after PKR 250,000 running costs is PKR 350,000 a month. PKR 4.2 million / 350,000 = 12 months. Seven months comes from ignoring running costs.

cards.title: Data readiness: the hidden make-or-break
cards.body:
An agent is only as good as the information and systems it can reach. Before committing, assess five areas.

**1. Access.** Can the agent reach the data through approved, secure routes such as APIs, read-only database views or system integrations? Screen-scraping legacy systems is fragile; manual exports go stale.

**2. Quality.** Are records complete, consistent and current? Duplicate customer records, free-text fields used inconsistently and missing values will confuse an agent just as they confuse new staff.

**3. Documented knowledge.** Are the rules and policies the agent must follow written down, current and owned? Many processes run on unwritten knowledge held by experienced staff. That knowledge has to be captured before an agent can use it.

**4. Examples with known outcomes.** Do you have past cases with correct outcomes to build the evaluation set? If historical decisions were inconsistent, you are teaching and testing against noise.

**5. Permissions and sensitivity.** Is the data classified? Do you know which data is personal, confidential or restricted, and who may see it? Can access rules be applied to what the agent retrieves?

Pakistani organisations often face specific issues: scanned rather than digital documents, mixed English, Urdu and Roman Urdu text, CNIC numbers entered in different formats, and core systems with limited integration options. None of these is a reason to give up, but each needs time and budget. A common rule of thumb in practice is that data and integration work takes a larger share of the effort than the AI components themselves.

cards.title: Build, buy or configure
cards.body:
There are three broad ways to get an agent into production.

| Option | What it means | Best when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Buy** a packaged agent | A vendor product built for a function, such as service desk or customer chat | The process is standard and the vendor's integrations fit your systems | Lock-in, limited control over data handling, generic behaviour, unclear evaluation |
| **Configure** a platform | Use an enterprise agent platform or the agent features of systems you already own, adding your tools, knowledge and rules | You need tailoring but not deep engineering; you have some technical staff | Platform limits, costs that grow with usage, skills to configure well |
| **Build** | Your team assembles models, tools, orchestration and guardrails | The process is a source of competitive advantage, highly specific, or data cannot leave your control | Need for scarce engineering skills, ongoing maintenance, longer time to value |

Questions that decide the choice:

- **Data location and control:** where will prompts, documents and logs be processed and stored? Can the vendor use your data to train models? For regulated firms, this can rule options in or out.
- **Integration:** does the option connect to your core systems, or will you spend most of the budget on connectors?
- **Evaluation and logs:** can you run your own test set and see full logs of every tool call?
- **Exit:** if you change provider, can you take your prompts, tools, knowledge index and logs with you?
- **Total cost over three years**, not just licence price.

Most organisations end up mixing options: buying where the process is standard and building or configuring where they need control or differentiation.

cards.title: Ask for the logs in the sales meeting
cards.body: When assessing any vendor agent, ask to see a **full trace of a real task**: every prompt, retrieved document, tool call, result and final output. If the product cannot show you this, you will not be able to investigate complaints, satisfy auditors or debug failures later. Also ask where each part of that trace is stored, for how long, and whether it is used for training.

cards.title: Running a pilot that proves something
cards.body:
Many AI pilots end in a pleasant demo and no decision. A good pilot is a controlled experiment designed to answer one question: **should we scale this, change it or stop it?**

**Design elements:**

- **Narrow scope:** one process, one channel, one or two case types, a defined user group (for example, ten officers in two branches).
- **Success criteria agreed in advance:** quality thresholds (accuracy, correct escalation), efficiency gains, user adoption, and hard limits such as 'zero unapproved write actions'.
- **Shadow mode first:** the agent processes real cases but its outputs are not used; staff work normally and results are compared. This tests quality with no customer risk.
- **Then assisted mode:** staff see and use the agent's output, at a low autonomy level.
- **A comparison group:** similar staff or cases without the agent, so you can separate the agent's effect from seasonal changes.
- **Enough duration and volume:** typically several weeks and hundreds of cases, including month-end peaks if relevant.
- **Exit criteria:** what result means scale, what means redesign, what means stop.

**What to record:** quality on the evaluation set and on live cases, time per case, staff feedback, failure types, cost per case, and any incidents.

Be ready for a pilot that says **stop**. A pilot that kills a weak idea quickly and cheaply has done its job. The failure is a pilot that runs for a year with no criteria and becomes a permanent, unscaled 'innovation project'.

cards.title: Use-case patterns across sectors
cards.body:
These patterns recur in Pakistani organisations. Each lists a typical starting autonomy level.

| Sector | Use case | What the agent does | Typical start |
|---|---|---|---|
| Banking | Customer onboarding pre-checks | Extracts data from CNIC and forms, checks completeness and consistency, flags gaps | Level 1 to 2 |
| Banking | Alert investigation support | Gathers transaction history, profile and news for an analyst; drafts a narrative | Level 1 |
| Banking | Trade document checking | Extracts and compares document data against credit terms | Level 1 to 3 per action |
| Telecom | Billing and bundle complaints | Checks usage and activation logs, issues small credits within limits, routes the rest | Level 2 to 3 |
| Telecom | Network fault triage | Correlates alarms and tickets, suggests likely cause and dispatches field teams | Level 1 to 2 |
| HR | Employee policy questions | Answers from current HR policies with citations, in English or Urdu | Level 3 for answers |
| HR | Onboarding coordination | Creates records and requests, chases missing documents | Level 2 to 3 |
| Customer service | Email and chat replies | Drafts or sends replies for routine queries; escalates complaints | Level 1, then 3 for simple intents |
| Procurement | Vendor onboarding | Checks registration and tax status documents, flags risks | Level 1 to 2 |

Notice what is absent: no agent makes final credit, disciplinary or large payment decisions alone. Those remain human, supported by agent-prepared information.

cards.question: A pilot of a claims-summary agent ran for six weeks. Staff liked it, but no success criteria were set and no comparison group was used. Turnaround improved 15%, during a period when claim volumes also fell. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: It cannot show how much came from the agent; rerun with criteria and a comparison
The agent caused the 15% improvement and should now be scaled to every claims team immediately
The agent should be stopped because pilots without criteria always fail
Staff satisfaction alone is enough evidence to scale
cards.explanation: Without a comparison group, the drop in volumes could explain the faster turnaround. The pilot produced positive signals but not evidence of the agent's effect. Stopping is not justified either; the design needs fixing.

cards.title: Chart Room take-aways
items: Start from painful work and waiting time, and redesign the process rather than automating a broken one.
Good candidates are high-volume, language-heavy, data-accessible, with detectable and reversible errors and known right answers.
Score ideas on value, feasibility and risk; build a portfolio of quick wins, a few strategic bets and reusable components.
Honest business cases include running costs, adoption ramps and a clear account of how saved hours become value.
Data access, quality, documented rules and permissions usually decide success more than model choice.
Pilots need narrow scope, criteria agreed upfront, shadow mode, a comparison group and exit rules.

cards.prompt: List three candidate agent use cases from your organisation and score each on value, feasibility and risk. Which would you pilot first, and what single success criterion would convince your leadership to scale it?

quiz.question: A process walk of SME loan processing at a Sialkot branch shows the credit officer's analysis takes 40 minutes, but files wait an average of six days for a missing document or an approver's signature. What should the team conclude first?
options: An agent that drafts the credit analysis in minutes will remove most of the six-day delay from turnaround time
The best solution is to replace the credit officer with an autonomous agent
AI cannot help with loan processing in any way
Most delay is waiting time, so the hand-offs and document chasing need fixing, not just the analysis
quiz.explanation: Speeding up a 40-minute step barely affects a six-day wait. The big gains lie in redesigning the hand-offs and in chasing documents, where an agent might also help. Replacing the officer ignores the real bottleneck and the risk.

quiz.question: Which process is the weakest candidate for an AI agent?
options: Answering staff questions about current HR policies from an owned, up-to-date policy library
Deciding annual bonuses for senior managers, done once a year with no agreed criteria
Checking vendor invoices against purchase orders, with thousands of invoices a month
Drafting replies to routine customer emails for review
quiz.explanation: Annual senior bonus decisions are rare, high-stakes, sensitive and lack agreed right answers, failing several screening tests at once. The other processes have volume, data and reviewable outputs.

quiz.question: A use case scores Value 5, Feasibility 2, Risk 4 in a prioritisation workshop. How should it be treated?
options: As a strategic bet: plan carefully, close feasibility gaps, start at low autonomy
As a quick win to launch this quarter, because the value score is the highest possible
As a filler to be done if time allows
As a use case to drop permanently
quiz.explanation: High value with low feasibility and high risk is a strategic bet. It is too hard and risky to be a quick win, too valuable to treat as a filler or drop, and suits a cautious, low-autonomy start.

quiz.question: An agent will resolve 40% of a telecom's 20,000 monthly queries end to end, each previously taking 5 minutes of staff time. Loaded staff cost is PKR 900 per hour, running costs are PKR 200,000 a month and the one-time cost is PKR 6 million. What is the simple payback at full run rate?
options: 10 months
30 months
15 months
7.5 months
quiz.explanation: Cases: 20,000 x 40% = 8,000; time: 8,000 x 5 = 40,000 minutes, about 666.7 hours, worth PKR 600,000. Net after PKR 200,000 running cost is PKR 400,000, so payback is PKR 6 million / 400,000 = 15 months. Ten months ignores running costs.

quiz.question: A business case claims PKR 30 million annual savings from an agent because it releases 25,000 staff hours a year. The department has no plans to reduce hiring or reassign staff. What is the main weakness?
options: The hourly cost used is probably too low, because it excludes benefits, overheads and supervision costs
Hours are capacity, not cash: no hiring is avoided and no redeployment is planned
Agents cannot realistically release as many as 25,000 hours a year in a single department of this size
Savings should be shown monthly, not annually
quiz.explanation: Hours released are capacity, not cash. Without a plan to avoid hiring, redeploy staff or capture quality benefits, the claimed savings will not appear. The other points do not address this core flaw.

quiz.question: Which item is most often left out of agent business cases, causing benefits to be overstated?
options: The cost of the initial pilot workshops, including facilitators and venue hire for business and IT teams
The cost of office space for the project team
The cost of printing user guides
Running costs such as model usage, monitoring, human review and ongoing maintenance
quiz.explanation: Running costs recur every month and grow with usage, so omitting them can change a case from strong to weak. The other items are small one-off costs.

quiz.question: An insurer in Karachi wants an agent to check motor claims against policy terms. Policy wordings exist only as scanned PDFs, several product versions are in force, and past claim decisions were inconsistent between regions. What should come first?
options: Start the agent immediately in production and let it learn from its mistakes and from staff corrections
Buy the most expensive model available to compensate for poor data
Digitise and version the wordings, agree consistent rules and a reviewed set of example cases
Use the historical decisions as the evaluation set as they are
quiz.explanation: The agent needs readable, versioned knowledge and a reliable ground truth. Inconsistent past decisions would make a misleading test set, and a better model cannot fix unreadable or conflicting sources.

quiz.question: A bank must keep customer data under strict control and wants an agent for a highly specific trade finance process that differentiates it from competitors. Packaged products process data in a foreign cloud and allow little customisation. Which option fits best?
options: Build or configure a solution on infrastructure that meets the bank's data requirements, accepting longer time to value
Buy the packaged product because it is fastest
Use a free consumer chat tool with staff pasting documents into it
Avoid AI entirely for trade finance
quiz.explanation: Data control needs and a differentiating, specific process favour building or configuring under the bank's control. The packaged product fails the data and customisation tests, and consumer tools pasted with customer documents create serious data leakage risk.

quiz.question: Which pilot design gives the most reliable evidence on whether a loan-document agent should be scaled?
options: Give the agent to all 200 branches at once to get the largest possible sample, and gather feedback after a week
Run a two-day demo for senior management using selected cases
Let the most enthusiastic officer use it for a month and report on how it felt
Shadow then assisted mode in a few branches for several weeks, with agreed criteria and a comparison group
